quote: To me, it seems inevitable that the capabilities of intelligent machines will increase not just because of physics but because we're starting to understand better and better how to get those machines to behave intelligently. So it wouldn't surprise me if it happened in my lifetime and I could easily imagine it happening in the lifetime of my children.

Read in full. Ambiguous: target_capability, since "it" refers back to systems more intelligent than humans getting beyond our control, not a named capability; coded superintelligence. Endorsement uncertain: "wouldn't surprise me" and "could easily imagine" are hedges, not a prediction. Agency from his next sentence in the same answer ("the sooner we start solving this problem, the better"), outside the stored quote, so the governance frame rests on context. Same interview: five years ago most AI people would have said human-level AI was "Decades and decades or centuries away", "but now I think it seems as if it's a little bit closer"; and he explains an intelligence explosion as a system at human level that "can redesign itself using better hardware and better algorithms".

notes: basis: "may sometimes be measured not in centuries"; Russell's contribution "Of Myths And Moonshine" to the Edge Reality Club conversation "The Myth of AI" (Jaron Lanier, conversation dated 11.14.14 on the page). Russell's reply is not dated on the page, so year precision only. Read in full at edge.org (fetched with curl). Mentions Rodney Brooks (a panel member) only as the target of the reply. quote: But if that problem is solved — and it's certainly not impossible — then we would see another big increase in machine capabilities. There are two or three problems like that where if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle between there and human-level AI.

definition_note: human-level AI
notes: basis: "if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle"; Quanta Magazine Q&A by Natalie Wolchover, "Concerns of an Artificial Intelligence Pioneer", dated April 21, 2015 on the page; read in full (fetched with curl). Reprinted by Wired 2015-05-23 (same text, not a separate row). present_capability disputed: just before, he says hierarchical decision making is "one of the missing pieces right now". Same interview: success "would be an enormous thing. 'The biggest event in human history'", earlier "Probably it was just too far away", and he explains the intelligence explosion as machines that "will be able to work on AI just like we do and improve their own capabilities" (he is describing the idea, not endorsing it).

quote: The arrival of AGI, he says, is not imminent, and he won't be drawn on a date: we can't predict when the breakthroughs which will get us there will happen, he insists. But they might not be many decades away.

notes: secondhand; basis: "they might not be many decades away"; Calum Chace's blog report (post dated May 16, 2015) of Russell's public lecture "The Long-Term Future of (Artificial) Intelligence" at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, Cambridge, on 15 May 2015 (date in the post and in Russell's own media list). The words are the blogger's paraphrase, not a direct quotation; a video of the talk exists (YouTube) but has no transcript, so not checked. Read at calumchace.com (fetched with curl); the page renders "not" and "they" with stray markup inside the words, normalised here. Endorsement uncertain: "might" with a vague horizon, plus an explicit refusal to give a date.

quote: “If we had computers a trillion times faster we wouldn’t have human-level AI; half in jest, one might say we’d just get wrong answers a trillion times sooner,” he says. “What matters are real conceptual and algorithmic breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict.”

timeline_text: breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict
definition_note: human-level AI
notes: Nature news feature by Declan Butler, "A world where everyone has a robot: why 2040 could blow your mind", published 24 February 2016 (date on nature.com); the reporter spoke to Russell, so elicitation interview, primary. nature.com now paywalls the piece; read at the Wayback Machine copy of the free 2016 news page (fetched with curl). Endorsement unexpressed: he rejects a route (raw computing speed) and says the breakthroughs are hard to predict, but does not say whether human-level AI will come (A15 ruling 4).

quote: Solving the safety problem well enough to move forward in AI seems to be feasible but not easy. There are probably decades to plan for the arrival of superintelligent machines. But the problem should not be dismissed out of hand, as it has been by some AI researchers.

timeline_text: There are probably decades to plan for the arrival

The PDF breaks "researchers" across a line with a hyphen; joined here. A14 ruling 11: decades away is accepts; "probably" is not one of the hedges (may, might, could) that make a date uncertain. Agency from "Solving the safety problem ... seems to be feasible". Same article: "Still others think that superintelligent AI will never happen", answered with the Rutherford and Szilard story, which argues against "never".

quote: somewhat more than half (67.5 percent) of Etzioni’s respondents plumped for “more than 25 years” to achieve superintelligence—after all, more than half of Bostrom’s respondents gave dates beyond 25 years for a mere 50 percent probability of achieving mere human-level intelligence. One of us (Russell) responded to Etzioni’s survey with “more than 25 years,”
claim_summary: Co-written reply to Oren Etzioni: Russell reports that he answered Etzioni's 2016 survey on when superintelligence will be achieved with 'more than 25 years'.

The unit is Russell's own survey answer, reported by himself; the survey was Etzioni's 2016 poll of AAAI fellows (published 2016-09-20), so the answer itself was given earlier in 2016; dated here by publication. Elicitation survey (answering a survey item), source_type blog because the source read is the opinion piece. A15 ruling 5: a minimum number of years asserts arrival with a minimum, so accepts with an open high bound; choosing "more than 25 years" rather than "never" supports that, and the piece adds Etzioni's headline "could just as easily have been '75 percent of experts think superintelligent AI is inevitable.'"

quote: The difficulty in predicting such breakthroughs means that giving any precise estimate of the date on which human-level AI will arrive is foolhardy. Nonetheless, most experts believe it is likely to arrive within the present century

notes: Russell's essay "Provably Beneficial Artificial Intelligence", in The Next Step: Exponential Life (BBVA OpenMind, 2017; citation from his own page; PDF metadata 2017-09-14), read in the copy on his Berkeley site through r.jina.ai. The text extraction splits the "ffi" letter group ("di ffi culty"); joined here. The sentence before the quote says more breakthroughs are needed "that we will not know how to describe until we see our best efforts to build general-purpose AI systems failing in interesting ways". present_capability disputed from the sentence just before: "Despite all this progress, we are still far from human-level AI." Same essay, answering the objection "Human-level AI is impossible": the claim "represents a foolhardy bet against human ingenuity"; and "The relevant timescale for human-level AI is less predictable, but of course that means it, like nuclear fission, might arrive considerably sooner than expected."

quote: reading is not yet happening in machines, at least with understanding. But that will happen, and when that happens, very soon afterwards, machines will have read everything that the human race has ever written. ... they'll be able to make better decisions in the real world than we can.

Read in the official TED transcript (page data fetched with curl). Article says "If a typical person can do a mental task with less than one second of thought, we can probably automate it using AI either now or in the near future" (narrow tasks, not coded). Judgment call: "far from" and "much more than" deny that current systems match human intelligence, so present_capability disputed; nothing is said about the future, so endorsement unexpressed (ruling 9).

quote: Since the early days of AI, people have wondered whether AI can ever be conscious or feel emotions. Even though an artificial general intelligence may be centuries away, these are important questions.

The letter is mainly about whether an AI can love or be conscious, which he calls philosophical questions; frame_primary is timeline because the only claim about AGI itself is its timing, and other_concern (consciousness) is present. "may" with "centuries" is a hedge, so uncertain (ruling 10); no number of centuries, so timeline_year blank.

quote: I continue to believe that some combination of learning algorithms, likely yet to be invented, will get us there someday.

Same letter: building AGI is "one of the grandest challenges of our time"; "Obviously, AGI would have extraordinary value"; he co-organized a NIPS 2005 workshop on human-level AI; ends "If you dream of making progress toward AGI yourself, I encourage you to keep dreaming!" Consequences, affect and agency are taken from those lines in the same letter, outside the stored quote; judgment call, so coding_confidence would be medium for those fields.

Same letter, later: "While AGI may be part of an indeterminate future, we have amazing capabilities today" (a hedge, not coded here because it is a separate passage; it would be uncertain).

quote: I believe that most people, including me, currently think of AGI as AI that can carry out any intellectual task that a human can. With this definition, I think we’re still at least decades away from AGI.

No number of decades is given, so timeline_year is left blank and the row is qualitative rather than a range; the lower_bound tag is not used because it needs a year. quote: Even though nontechnical pundits talk about “the race to AGI” as if AGI were a discrete technology to be invented, the reality is that AI technology will progress continuously ... Judgment call: he does not say AGI will never come, only that a declaration of it would be a marketing claim; present_capability disputed reads that as disputing any such claim, endorsement unexpressed.

quote: I look at how complex the training recipes are and how manual AI training and development is today, and there’s no way this is going to take us all the way to AGI just by itself,

quote: Modern AI is a general purpose technology that is enabling many applications, but AI that can do any intellectual tasks that a human can (a popular definition for AGI) is still decades away or longer.

quote: We shouldn’t buy into the inaccurate hype that LLMs are a path to AGI in just a few years, but we also shouldn’t buy into the opposite, also inaccurate hype that they are only demoware.

The claim rejects both a route (language models) and a near date; under A15 ruling 4 a route claim alone would be unexpressed, but here the timing ("in just a few years") is what he calls inaccurate, so coded rejects for that horizon only. No not_by tag because "a few years" gives no year (2025 + a few). He does not say whether AGI comes later (see ng-2025-04, "decades away or longer").

quote: “AGI” has turned into a term of hype rather than a term with a precise meaning. A reasonable definition of AGI is AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can. definition_note: AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can; tested by doing a work task as well as a skilled human (Turing-AGI Test)
notes: The Batch issue 334 (New Year issue) letter, published 2026-01-02; the panel verification's latest statement for him. Same letter: CEOs sometimes assume "AI will be more capable in 1-2 years than any likely reality"; hype risks a bubble; "If we run a Turing-AGI Test competition and every AI system falls short, that will be a good thing!" Consequence (economic, harmful: a bubble) and agency (a test can recalibrate expectations) come from the same letter, outside the stored quote. No position on when AGI arrives, so endorsement unexpressed.

quote: We are closer than before, yet many decades away from an AI that matches human intelligence.

Same interview: he expects robots throughout everyday life within 50 years (not about human-level AI).

quote: Eventually, we will create truly artificial intelligences, with cognition and consciousness recognizably similar to our own. I have no idea how, exactly, this creation will come about. Endorsement: the unit says it will come eventually and not before 2030, so accepts with the hedge in timeline_text (codebook: rejecting a near date while accepting eventual arrival). Same essay: "The singularity will be a period, not an event" and "machines will become gradually more intelligent, generation by generation" (the same capability, not split).

quote: In order for there to be a successful volitional AI, especially one that could be successfully malevolent, it would need a direct understanding of the world ... It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work from thousands of scientists and engineers. And, most likely, centuries.

definition_note: volitional or intentional artificially intelligent beings; elsewhere in the essay, human level or super human level intelligence
notes: basis: "It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work"; Own essay, first published on the Rethink Robotics blog and reposted on Robohub under his byline; read at Robohub; date from the Robohub byline (11 November 2014). timeline_year left blank: "centuries" gives no number (codebook ruling 11 by analogy with decades). Same essay: "it is a mistake to be worrying about us developing malevolent AI anytime in the next few hundred years" and "Moore's Law applied to this very real technical advance will not by itself bring about human level or super human level intelligence" (a route claim). Target judgment: volitional AI read as broad competence.

quote: The fears of runaway AI systems either conquering humans or making them irrelevant are not even remotely well grounded. Misled by suitcase words, people are making category errors in fungibility of capabilities. These category errors are comparable to seeing more efficient internal combustion engines appearing and jumping to the conclusion that warp drives are just around the corner.

Date: the page gives only the question year 2015, so year precision. elicitation survey because it answers a question put to many contributors; source_type blog is the nearest value for a short signed essay. Ambiguous fields: endorsement and frame. The warp-drive analogy says runaway AI is nowhere near, but the words do not say whether it will ever exist, so endorsement is unexpressed; timeline is present only through the analogy.

quote: "We are going to have more robots, we are going to have more artificial intelligence, but I think people are misinterpreting the progress that is being made," he said. "I don't think we have to worry about that in our lifetime or our children's lifetimes."
